19777-aids-to-the-study-of-the-maya-codi:
Only a handful of Maya codices, painted folding books, survived the Spanish conquest. Aids to the Study of the Maya Codices appeared in the Sixth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology. Its author, Cyrus Thomas, offers finds not in his earlier papers. He calls the field American paleography, the reading of native manuscripts. Every glyph read was hard won.

Thomas worked when Maya writing was still mostly unread. His aids recorded signs, calendars, and picture sequences for other scholars. Some of his readings later proved wrong, as pioneers' work does. The report still marks a step toward decipherment. It shows federal science funding deep-time American studies. Students of the Maya can watch the field learning to see.
19827-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for June 1864 is volume 13, number 80. The Civil War was entering its fourth summer as this issue appeared. One piece turns on the flattery of fishing guides. The writer confesses his affections were caught in a net of silken flattery. Your good guide, your dear guide, he jokes, knows the sport of praise. Such light essays shared pages with war news.

Boston's Atlantic served the Union's educated readers. It printed Holmes, Lowell, and the era's best pens. A monthly number balances grave and gay on purpose. June 1864 readers needed both registers badly. The magazine's mix is itself a historical record. It shows a literary culture holding together under war strain.
20527-the-sherwood-foresters-in-the-grea:
The Sherwood Foresters in the Great War is the history of the regiment's 1/8th Battalion in the First World War. The battalion came from Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire. Its war is traced through maps and plans of the Western Front.

The maps list tells the battalion's road. There are plans of the Gorre Brewery and the Clock Tower at Béthune, and of the St. Quentin Canal at Bellenglise. Other sheets cover Kemmel, Hooge, the Hohenzollern Redoubt, Gommecourt, and Lens. Unit histories like this one kept faith with the men who served and fell.
20624-ballads-of-scottish-tradition-and-:
Ballads of Scottish Tradition and Romance gathers Scotland's old popular ballads: border raids, true loves, and tragedies in verse. It belongs to the same series as the English ballad volumes, with texts chosen and edited with care. Reviewers praised the work warmly.

There can be nothing but praise, said the Academy, for the selection, editing, and notes, which are all excellent and adequate. It is, in fine, a valuable volume of what bids fair to be a very valuable series. The ballads themselves — of Tam Lin, the border reivers, and drowned lovers — carry the old music of Scotland.
20839-the-mountain-chant-a-navajo-ceremo:
Branches, darkness, and a great fence of pinon limbs close the Mountain Chant's last night. Washington Matthews names the rite ilnasjingo qacal, the chant in the dark circle of branches. A corral of boughs takes in guests and singers after sunset.

Matthews, an army surgeon, recorded this Navajo ceremony with rare care. Chants, sand paintings, dances, and myths fill the fifth annual report study. He learned the Navajo tongue and won the singers' trust. The work stays a key record of a healing rite, kept in detail that later scholars still mine today.
21071-the-rover-s-secret-a-tale-of-the-p:
Pirates haunt the cays and lagoons of Cuba in Harry Collingwood's tale of the Rover's secret. The Rover himself is a pirate who appears through the story without the word rover ever being used in the main text. Wounded to death, he saves his secret for the final chapter.

That deathbed telling explains several puzzles the reader has met along the way. Around it Collingwood builds a Caribbean tale of lagoons, hiding places, and old piracy in his usual flowing style. The prose is ornate and long-winded at times, as his fans expected, but the delayed secret holds the plot together.
21204-the-recent-revolution-in-organ-bui:
George Laing Miller, a Fellow of the Royal College of Organists, surveyed the rapid changes in organ building here. The book first appeared in 1909 and was reissued in a second edition in 1913. Miller had played organs in England and America, including Christ Church, Pelham Manor, New York. His frontispiece shows the great Willis organ in St George's Hall, Liverpool.

The opening chapter, As It Was, sets the old organ against the new machinery: pneumatic levers, wind chests, and modern actions. Miller explains the new parts with photographs and diagrams. For organists of the time, it was a guide to instruments that were changing under their hands.
21274-the-american-cyclops-the-hero-of-n:
Pasquino, a pen name borrowed from Rome's talking statue, published this satire at Baltimore in 1868. Its target is General Benjamin Butler, the American Cyclops of the title. Butler had ruled occupied New Orleans, where his order on silver spoons and his treatment of the city's women made him hated across the South. The pamphlet dubs him spoiler of silver spoons.

Its introduction retells Ulysses and Polyphemus, with the modern Cyclops bottled up, the saucy rebel Beauregard keeping him sealed. Verses picture a pot-house soldier, bold by day and drunk by night. Illustrated and bitter, it is a piece of post-Civil War political abuse in classical dress.
21341-practical-english-composition-book:
Book Two of this school composition course serves the second year of English study, and its directions begin before any theme is written. When a corrected theme comes back, the student must number each correction and circle it heavily. On a fresh sheet the student states the error, corrects it, and gives the reason. Word misuse, repetition, and weak ideas each get named.

Lessons then build themes step by step, with a poem on metrical feet helping students hear rhythm in prose and verse. The method is strict: answer the critic's questions, follow suggestions, and hand the correction sheet in proper form. It preserves the drill-based composition teaching of its era in full working order.
21461-fred-markham-in-russia-or-the-boy-:
Fred Markham and his brother tour Russia with Cousin Giles in W. H. G. Kingston's Fred Markham in Russia. Giles, a naval officer hurt out of service, invites them in 1856. Their mother is glad the trip stays closer than the far side of the world.

After a rough sea crossing, the boys see Saint Petersburg and travel wider. New friends tell long tales of their own lives under the Czars. Through those tales Kingston teaches much about Russian customs, rule, and hardship. The boys find thrills of their own as well, and the book mixes travel fact with story in Kingston's known way.
21814-the-trial-and-death-of-jesus-chris:
James Stalker, a Scottish minister and writer on the life of Jesus, walks slowly through the Passion in this devotional history of 1894. The study begins where Jesus falls into the hands of justice, at the gate of Gethsemane at midnight. Chapters follow the arrest, the church trial, Peter's denial, and the civil trial before Pilate.

Stalker prints the Gospel texts at each chapter head, drawing on all four evangelists. Herod, the crown of thorns, Judas, and the way of the cross each get their own close study. The closing chapters rest at Calvary and the words from the cross. He writes for believers who want the story told in order, with feeling and care. It is devotion built on the text itself.
21902-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for May 1866, the hundred-and-third number of America's leading literary magazine, opens with The Harmonists. Its narrator measures himself against his brother Josiah, a successful attorney in a manufacturing town. Josiah belongs to the ruling class of slow eyes and bull-dog jaws. The narrator watches him, and the great market, from an odd little corner. Price-marks, he fears, are stamped on all things now.

The issue carries the magazine's usual mix of literature, science, art, and politics. Ticknor and Fields published it in Boston in the first spring after the Civil War. The Atlantic was then the voice of America's literary establishment. One monthly number preserves its tone exactly: reflective essays and stories from the pens that shaped the nation's reading.
22915-the-new-land-stories-of-jews-who-h:
Elma Ehrlich Levinger's The New Land, published in 1920, tells stories of Jews who helped make America. Her preface notes what the histories leave out. Peter Stuyvesant's hostility to Jews is well documented, she writes. Yet no history mentions the Jewish boy who hoped to play with the governor's young niece. A Jewish soldier who saved a Tory from a mob also went unrecorded.

Levinger fills those gaps with tales for young readers, from colonial days forward. Gallant young Franks, friend of George Washington, stands among her heroes. The book argues, story by story, that Jewish Americans belong in the national tale from its start. It remains a warm piece of educational storytelling with a clear purpose.
23041-the-works-of-william-shakespeare-c:
Scholarship explains itself in the first volume of the Cambridge edition of Shakespeare's Works. The editors promise the full results of their comparisons in footnotes. Proposed corrections from themselves and their correspondents appear there too. The reader thus gets, in compact form, a complete view of the materials from which the text has been constructed.

That promise made the Cambridge Shakespeare a landmark of Victorian editing when it appeared in the 1860s. Volume one opens the comedies with texts built by comparing the earliest printings line by line. The notes let any reader watch the editors choose between readings. For students of how Shakespeare reached modern pages, this apparatus is the story, as gripping as the plays it serves.
bygone-beliefs-being-a-series-of-excursi: H. Stanley Redgrove's 1920 tour of old superstitions and secret wisdom: alchemy, astrology, magic, and the philosopher's stone. govdocs-archive_org-TheInteriorCastleOrT:
St. Teresa of Ávila, the Spanish Carmelite nun and mystic, wrote The Interior Castle in 1577. In it she pictures the soul as a castle made of a single diamond, with seven sets of rooms, or mansions, leading inward toward God at the center.

Each mansion marks a stage of prayer and growth, from beginners distracted by the world outside the walls to souls united with God in the innermost room. Teresa describes the trials of each stage from her own experience, in plain and vivid images. The book remains a classic of Christian mystical writing, read far beyond the convent walls.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JournalofForens:
Don Olson and Ralph F. Turner published an article in the Journal of Forensic Sciences in October 1971 on photographic evidence in the assassination of President Kennedy. Their subject is the pictures themselves: the films and photographs taken in Dealey Plaza, treated as forensic material rather than as illustrations.

Photographs were the case's most trusted and most fought-over witnesses. A forensic journal gave their study the standing of science. Olson and Turner examine what the images can and cannot establish, in the language of their profession. The article preserves that professional reading for researchers of the evidence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RPTOfDoJTaskFor:
A Department of Justice task force wrote this report on domestic security investigations. It sets out the bases on which such investigations may be opened: force, violence, or violations of federal law. It then gives the guidelines that govern how the work is done. The report belongs to the King and Ray side of these files, where security investigations were reviewed after the fact.

After the abuses of the Hoover years were exposed, the department had to write its rules down. A task force report is where that writing happened. This one preserves the standards the department set for itself: what justifies opening a file on Americans, and what limits the investigators. Readers can measure the era's practice against the era's own stated rules.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
In November 1985, guerrillas seized Colombia's Palace of Justice in Bogotá, and the army's retaking left the building in ruins. This briefing book, edited by Michael Evans and posted in September 2023, covers the United States role around that tragedy. Its title calls the month Black November.

The posting urges Colombia's President Gustavo Petro to follow a 2014 ruling of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. That ruling concerned people who vanished during the retaking and the duties Colombia still owes their families. Declassified American records supply Washington's view of the siege and its long legal shadow.

In 1993 a Colombian senator walked into the United States Embassy with a serious claim. He said the founders of the Medellín drug cartel had financed the Senate campaign of Álvaro Uribe Vélez. This briefing book, posted in May 2018, publishes the documents behind that claim.

Uribe later became president of Colombia, which is why a 1993 embassy report still matters. The posting's nickname, Narcopols, points to politicians tied to drug money. Readers should note what the record is: a senator's statement recorded by diplomats, preserved in American files and released long afterward.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-int:
Ernesto "Che" Guevara was executed in the hills of Bolivia at 1:15 in the afternoon on October 9, 1967. He had been captured by a Bolivian military battalion trained by the United States. This briefing book was posted fifty-three years later, in October 2020.

The Argentine-born revolutionary had gone to Bolivia to start a guerrilla campaign, and the CIA tracked that campaign closely. A documentary record of the hunt shows both sides of it: the small band in the mountains and the intelligence effort watching them. It remains a core file on how Guevara's last campaign ended.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_environm: Operation Crossroads was the first postwar atomic test series, held at Bikini Atoll in July 1946. govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: In January 1986 Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev proposed a sweeping nuclear initiative, a staged plan toward eliminating nuclear weapons. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the documents are not described. The initiative matters because it showed a Soviet leader bidding for abolition in public, which changed the politics every later arms negotiation inherited.

Additional Protocol I, added to the Geneva Conventions in the 1970s, set new humanitarian rules for warfare. The United States and its NATO allies reviewed it from 1978 to 1986. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in September 2023, on that review and its outcome.

The Reagan administration rejected the agreement. Pentagon objections proved insurmountable, and officials believed the protocol favored terrorists. That rejection has shaped American war law ever since, since later administrations kept the same distance. The declassified collection shows an alliance debating the rules of war on paper while the Cold War's arsenals stood ready.

Do the laws of war limit nuclear weapons, and how? William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in June 2023, on that question in American records. It gathers declassified material on legal thinking about the bomb.

Evidence here is brief, so claims stay general. The subject itself is significant: lawyers inside government had to fit a weapon of mass destruction into rules written for ordinary battle. Those internal debates shape targeting policy and official statements to this day. Readers interested in where law meets the arsenal will find the primary paper in one place.

MIGHTY DERRINGER was a United States nuclear exercise held in 1986, part of the regular rehearsals of how a nuclear war would be commanded and fought. This briefing-book page presents the Archive's record of that exercise. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, so the exercise documents cannot be described. Exercises like this matter to historians because they show the war plan as practiced, not just as written. They record who would be called and what would be simulated. SIOP-64, the American nuclear war plan of the mid-1960s, contained an option aimed at destroying China and the Soviet Union as viable societies. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 638, published in August 2018, in a series revisiting the SIOP. The plan set expected damage levels of ninety-five percent.

Pre-delegation instructions, which let commanders act if Washington was destroyed, excluded Yugoslavia from the attack on Sino-Soviet nations. That small exception shows planners sorting communist states even inside a plan for general war. The documents expose overkill as written policy: not excess in the heat of battle, but percentages fixed in advance by planners.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Previously secret transcripts of summit meetings between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev, held from 1985 to 1988, anchor a book announced by the National Security Archive in December 2016. The volume, published with Central European University Press, adds George H. W. Bush's later talks with Gorbachev, from 1989 through 1991, so both sides of the table speak in their own words.

Read side by side, the Soviet and American records show Gorbachev pushing what the Archive calls an arms race in reverse. Reagan urges quiet talk on human rights rather than public pressure. Bush at first seeks new nuclear weapons, then comes around to cuts near the end. For readers, the paired transcripts show how the Cold War ended in the room, not just in speeches.

Memorial spent more than thirty years recording the crimes of the Soviet era, naming victims and keeping their stories alive in Russia. In March 2022, as Russian troops invaded Ukraine, the Russian Supreme Court rejected the group's appeal and let shutdown orders stand. The National Security Archive posted this account of that legal end, called a liquidation.

The posting ties two stories together: a state moving to erase memory of past repression while starting a new war. Memorial's fate shows how space for honest history had closed inside Russia by 2022. For readers, the piece is a short record of what was lost when the country's best-known human rights group was shut down, and why archivists abroad preserved the news of it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
Under Argentina's military dictatorship of 1976 to 1983, secret detention centers held prisoners who were tortured and often killed. A National Security Archive posting gathers material on those centers, including testimony from survivors of the site Argentines remember as a house of horrors.

Survivor accounts carry weight that official files cannot, because the regime hid its crimes and denied the prisons existed. Placed beside declassified records, the testimony helps pin down what happened inside rooms the state meant to keep invisible. Readers interested in how evidence of a dirty war gets rebuilt, piece by piece, will find the human core of that work here.
letters-of-franz-liszt-volume-1-from-par: Franz Liszt wrote home constantly during his years on the road. This first volume of his letters carries the subtitle "From Paris to Rome: Years of Travel as a Virtuoso." La Mara collected the letters and prepared them for publication. Constance Bache made the English translation readers use here. Only the Project Gutenberg header survives in the hosted sample, so this note sticks to those title page facts.
letters-to-his-son-1748-on-the-fine-art-:
Chesterfield's letters of 1748 find his son studying at Leipzig. A letter of January 2 praises the boy's well-filled days. His time runs full from morning to night, his father notes.

Such use of time, Chesterfield says, is having it all to yourself. Well-laid hours pay immense interest within a few years. Even dull companions can teach a young man something, he hints. Fourteen table companions shared his son's meals at Leipzig. The year's letters mix study plans with worldly strategy. Leipzig's university drew students from across Protestant Europe. The son's routine there mixes languages, fencing, and society.
letters-to-his-son-1749-on-the-fine-art-:
In a letter of January 10, 1749, Chesterfield thanks his son warmly. The son's thanks for a present outdid the gift itself, he says. What matters is the use the boy will make of it.

Due attention to a book's inside, and contempt for its outside, comes next. That balance marks a man of sense, Chesterfield teaches. He then explains his plans for the boy's future expenses. The son is entering the world a little more now. Money, manners, and judgment fill this year's counsel. Presents and allowances recur in these practical letters. Chesterfield treats money as a lesson in self-command.
letters-to-his-son-1750-on-the-fine-art-:
A London letter of January 8, 1750, turns to religion and morality. Chesterfield admits he has seldom written on those subjects. His son's own reason, he trusts, gives true notions of both.

Mr. Harte, the boy's tutor, stands ready with precept and example. Chesterfield confines himself to the appearances of religion and morality. Decency, utility, and necessity require keeping those appearances, he argues. That cool advice made the letters famous and notorious at once. Readers still debate whether he taught virtue or only its surface. Mr. Harte later appears often as a trusted guide. Religion here means conduct more than doctrine for Chesterfield.
letters-to-his-son-1751-on-the-fine-art-:
Chesterfield's 1751 letters follow his son's debut in Paris. A January letter calls the debut a good one. The young man has entered good company, his father hears.

He must not sink into bad company, Chesterfield warns. Shyness makes most Englishmen strangers where they might be intimate. General invitations to supper should be used, with decency. Lord Albemarle's house offers one such open door. Paris becomes the classroom where earlier Leipzig lessons meet real society. Parisian suppers taught manners no book could give. Chesterfield urges ease without familiarity's common faults. Frequent the best houses, he urges, and learn by watching. Ease in company, once gained, opens every other door.
letters-to-his-son-1752-on-the-fine-art-:
A London letter of January 2, 1752, attacks laziness of mind. Inattention, Chesterfield says, harms knowledge as much as incapacity. A man who will not learn differs from one who cannot only in blame.

Many capable people never even ask for knowledge, he laments. Young English travelers abroad draw his special scorn here. They waste fine chances through incuriosity and ease. His son must instead question, observe, and take pains. This year's letters press industry as the base of every grace. He praises questions as the sign of a living mind. Travel, he insists, rewards only the traveler who looks.
nasa-tm-19630004027-some-aerodynamic-and:
Frank L. Clark and Joanna M. Evans of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-338, in November 1960. It studies craft shapes meant to glide back from space. These lifting reentry shapes were tested at steep angles of attack. Angles ran up to ninety degrees, fully sideways to the wind.

The tests ran at Mach 2.91, near three times sound's speed. The team measured air forces and how well controls worked. A lifting shape could steer its fall and land like a plane. That promise drove much early work on winged spacecraft. Clark and Evans gave designers hard numbers on control at angles no normal plane would ever fly.
nasa-tm-19650019820-effect-on-surface-th:
Herman Mark, Ralph D Sommers, and Michael J Mirtich at Lewis Research Center prepared this paper for a January 1965 meeting in New York. Tiny meteoroid grains strike spacecraft surfaces at great speed. Over time, those hits can change how a surface handles heat. The team reproduced that exposure in a controlled way, using very small fast particles.

A surface that absorbs or sheds heat differently can upset a spacecraft's temperature balance. Calibrated exposure means the test dose is known and measured. The study links that known dose to changes in thermal properties. Designers of long-lived spacecraft needed such data to predict how surfaces age in orbit.
nasa-tm-19650022587-low-temperature-mech:
W R Morgan, at Marshall Space Flight Center, measured how a strong steel alloy sheet behaves in deep cold for this July 23, 1965, report. The alloy is HP 9-4-25, a nickel-cobalt martensitic steel. Sheet about a sixteenth of an inch thick was tested from room heat down to the cold of liquid hydrogen temperatures.

Morgan found that both ultimate tensile strength and yield strength were considerably greater at the cold end. Cold can also make some metals brittle, so full data matter. Rocket tanks and lines hold fuels at such extreme cold. Designers need measured properties, not guesses, for the metals that contain them.
nasa-tm-19660012403-transonic-aerodynami:
Edward J Ray and Robert T Taylor at Langley tested a model supersonic airliner with no tail in a wind tunnel, for this March 1966 report. Speeds were transonic, around the speed of sound. The model had a fixed wing, rather than a swing wing. A tailless layout cuts weight and drag, but it must still stay stable and controllable at low speed.

The pair report the model's aerodynamic characteristics through that tricky speed range. Supersonic transports were a major design goal of the era. Tunnel data on bold layouts like this one showed which ideas deserved more work. Ray and Taylor give the measured base for judging the tailless transport concept.
nasa-tm-19660016087-a-calculation-method:
John D Warmbrod, in Marshall's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory, presented a full calculation method in this April 12, 1966, report for blunt bodies tipped with glass. On entry into an atmosphere, a blunt body's nose heats fiercely. A glass tip melts and flows away, carrying heat with it. That wearing away is called ablation. Warmbrod's method computes the flight path and the ablation at the nose point.

Both results are needed together, since the path sets the heating and the heating sets the loss. His method is given in detail for other engineers to use. Glass-tipped shapes were studied for entry vehicles that must survive a short, brutal heating pulse.
nasa-tm-19660020011-apollo-spacecraft-bp:
Kennedy Space Center's planning and technical support staff compiled this day-by-day record of Apollo spacecraft BP-15. BP-15 was a boilerplate spacecraft, a full-weight stand-in used for ground tests. The chronology runs from the arrival of its service module and adapter through the postlaunch report, per the catalog note. Each step of technical progress at the center is entered in order.

Chronologies preserve who did what, and when, in a huge program. Later questions about a test or a fault can be answered from such a record. Boilerplate flights tested launch and recovery steps without risking a flight-ready craft. The BP-15 record shows Kennedy Space Center learning its Apollo work piece by piece.
nasa-tm-19660030642-a-preface-to-the-non:
A. Temkin, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, offers this July 1966 paper as a preface, a set of first steps. Its subject is what happens when an electron strikes a hydrogen atom hard enough to knock another electron free. That process is called ionization, and Temkin treats it with nonadiabatic theory.

He gives preliminary considerations and solves a simpler first version of the problem. That solution points to a threshold law for how ionization starts. His results show a strong suppression of cases where the two outgoing electrons share energy equally. Extending the results deepens that suppression near equal energies, setting up the fuller theory to come.
nasa-tm-19670009329-kirchhoff-s-theorem-:
L. A. Chernov wrote this acoustics paper in Russian, published in 1950 in the proceedings of the acoustics commission of the Soviet Academy of Sciences. The English translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, in January 1967. It extends Kirchhoff's theorem, a workhorse result in acoustics and optics, to sound traveling through a moving medium.

An earlier generalization by Blokhintsev covered only a uniform flow. Chernov pushes the theorem further, to a medium in potential motion, a broader class of flows. He starts from the refined wave equation for such motion credited to Andreyev and Blokhintsev. After proving an auxiliary lemma, he shows the theorem at work on a concrete problem: a point source of sound sitting inside the flow.
nasa-tm-19670009414-numerical-techniques:
Theodore Katsanis wrote this work as a thesis at the Case Institute of Technology in June 1967. His advisor was Professor Milton Lees. The subject is a class of math problems called symmetric positive linear differential equations. Such equations turn up often in engineering work.

Katsanis develops a finite difference method for solving them. A finite difference method replaces smooth change with small steps a computer can handle. He builds the method to suit the special structure of these equations. The thesis gives later engineers a worked-out recipe for this family of problems.
nasa-tm-19670022198-full-scale-flight-te:
Willard S. Blanchard Jr. and James L. Raper, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, wrote this memorandum in October 1960. It reports a full-scale free flight test, launched from sea level, of the abort-escape system for a Project Mercury capsule. The system existed to pull a crewed capsule to safety if its booster failed at or just after takeoff.

The test article matched the real capsule and escape system at full size. An escape tower with its rocket motor sat atop the capsule, and a small drogue parachute deployed the large landing parachute. The escape system performed satisfactorily, the authors report, reaching a maximum altitude of 1,950 feet. The main parachute gave a steady sinking rate of about twenty-eight feet per second. Accelerations stayed within the tolerance of a properly positioned and supported human. Noise inside the uninsulated capsule peaked near 144 decibels during motor thrust.
nasa-tm-19670022199-design-and-experimen:
Robert R. Nunamaker, Donald A. Petrash, and Charles A. Wasserbauer, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, tested turbine blade changes in this investigation. The turbine is a high-weight-flow, low-pressure-ratio, single-stage machine. It was meant for a turbojet engine designed to cruise at four times the speed of sound.

The original rotor blades were thin, tall, and slightly tapered, which raised mechanical worries. One fix pinned neighboring blades together near the tips for support. That version ran below its design efficiency and missed the design flow. The second fix redesigned the blade for strength, and it cost essentially nothing in performance.
nasa-tm-19670026973-an-analysis-of-the-m:
James O. Ballance, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this analysis on July 31, 1967. It examines the molecular kinetics of the thermosphere probe. That probe measured gas temperature and density high in the atmosphere, where air is so thin that molecules rarely collide.

Ballance ran a Monte Carlo computer analysis of the free molecular flow. He calculated the transmission probability that links the outside density to the measured density. His simplified model matched measured signals well, except at high angles of attack. The results also suggested incoming molecules bounced at most once, if at all.
nasa-tm-19670028445-the-use-of-dsl-90-fo:
R. A. Lewallen and H. H. Trauboth, of the Computation Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on June 28, 1967. It tests a digital simulation language called DSL/90. Their test problem is the dynamics of a stabilized platform, the gimbaled base that keeps guidance instruments steady.

The authors set out to get a feel for the power of the language. The catalog record specifies the application: simulation of the Saturn guidance system's stabilized platform. A guidance platform must hold its orientation while the rocket moves around it. Showing that DSL/90 could model such motion proved the language on a real engineering problem.
nasa-tm-19680001615-effect-of-axial-flow:
Howard A. Stine, Velvin R. Watson, and Charles E. Shepard, of Ames Research Center in California, studied an electric arc blown by its own gas stream. They presented the work in Belgium in September 1964. The arc is wall-constricted, held narrow by the tube around it, with gas flowing along its axis.

Their study mixes experiment with theory. It covers sizes and pressures where radiation carries off a noticeable share of the energy. New numerical calculations are compared with older analytic ones and with the measurements. The two theories differ in detailed behavior, they find. Yet both give essentially the same overall picture, matching the experiments.
nasa-tm-19680012471-aerodynamic-characte:
Odell A. Morris and Milton Lamb, at the Langley Research Center in Virginia, compared two odd supersonic shapes in the unitary plan wind tunnel. One model wore a half-ring wing; the other, a swept wing. Both sat on the same kind of wide, flat body, with swappable nose and tail sections.

Tests ran from Mach 2.16 to Mach 3.70, measuring pitch behavior. Both shapes gained favorable extra lift from interference at zero angle of attack. The ring wing gained the most. Yet the swept wing won the best lift-to-drag scores, because its lift grew faster with angle. Changing nose and tail shapes made no real difference to those best scores.
nasa-tm-19680013884-capillary-rise-in-th:
Raymond F. Lacovic and James A. Berns of the Lewis Research Center wrote this May 1968 NASA memorandum, numbered TM X-1558. Their subject is capillary rise, the pull that draws liquid up a narrow gap, in the ring-shaped space between two concentric cylinders. The case they study is the fuel sensing gear aboard Atlas-Centaur rockets during quiet coast periods.

Flight data from three Atlas-Centaur missions gave the rise height over time at very low gravity levels. The longest coast lasted well over twenty minutes, far beyond earlier drop tower tests. The authors matched the flight data with a math formula that, in their words, accurately described the flow. Their work extended capillary studies to cold rocket fuels such as liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen.
nasa-tm-19680023734-the-latitudinal-temp:
H. G. Mayr, L. H. Brace, and W. Crevier of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this June 1968 report, X-621-68-233. Their subject is the topside ionosphere, the upper part of the charged layer high above Earth. They ask how its electron temperature changes from the equator toward the poles, and whether theory can match satellite readings.

Solving the energy and flow equations for two ion types reproduced the observed pattern up to sixty degrees of latitude. The match showed a cool trough at the equator and warm peaks at middle latitudes. Beyond sixty degrees the theory ran too cold. The authors suggest missing light ions there slow electron cooling, which would lift the real temperature.
nasa-tm-19690013568-an-investigation-of-:
Roger K. Crouch and Gerald D. Walberg of Langley Research Center investigated Avcoat 5026-39/M in this April 1969 memorandum, TM X-1778. Avcoat forms the reentry heat shield of the Apollo command module. The glass-filled plastic chars and wears away in a controlled fashion, carrying heat off with it. The pair tested it far beyond normal Apollo conditions.

Three high-enthalpy wind tunnels at Langley supplied a wide range of pressures, heating, and oxygen flows. Behavior depended strongly on the heat-transfer level, the summary states. At low levels the char wore back about as diffusion theory predicted. At high levels the wear rate climbed fast, and severe mechanical char failure appeared. Oxygen shaped the char only under the gentler conditions.
nasa-tm-19690014407-a-study-from-kinemat:
James B. Eades and George H. Wyatt of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this March 1969 preprint, X-643-69-106, on the kinematics of intercept and pursuit. Kinematics studies motion itself, apart from the forces behind it. Their problems are flat, two-dimensional ones: how should one moving vehicle steer to reach another?

The pair treat the questions from both mathematical and physical viewpoints, with worked examples throughout. Cases include the simple straight-line intercept and pursuit of a target on a straight path. A harder case has the target flying a circular path. Alongside each path they give flight time, range history, and the acceleration the chasing vehicle must endure. Ample graphs picture what happens during each maneuver.
nasa-tm-19690029468-an-experimental-and-:
Billy Grant McKinney of Marshall Space Flight Center studied water heat pipes for moderate temperature ranges in this report, TM X-53849. Heat pipes move heat with no moving parts, suiting spacecraft thermal control well. His working range ran from about two hundred to three hundred fifty degrees Fahrenheit, tested in steady operation.

Sixteen pipes were investigated near the vertical: eight as radiating fins, eight with an insulated section and condenser. Instruments recorded heat inputs, surface and interior temperatures, and pressures throughout. Governing equations were programmed so permeability, contact angle, and section length effects could be studied. McKinney also gives screen wick permeability results and an assembly method that keeps the vapor space clean.
nasa-tm-19700025395-apollo-mission-f-per:
Rendezvous charts for Mission F get a performance analysis in this Houston internal note, dated April 29, 1969. Mission F was Apollo 10, the last full rehearsal before the first landing. The charts guided the lunar module's meeting with the command module in lunar orbit after its descent rehearsal.

The analysis sets out its study rules, the digital program used, and the charts themselves. Starting conditions come next, along with errors allowed in sensors and in how burns were carried out. Braking schedules and line-of-sight rate limits round out the setup. Results then report maneuver values, miss distance, fuel used in small correction burns, and arrival timing.
nasa-tm-19700026532-the-concept-of-gener:
Henry P. Decell Jr. wrote this mathematics paper on the generalized inversion of complex matrices. Some matrices have no normal inverse, yet a generalized inverse can still serve in their place. The concept matters wherever large sets of equations must be solved by computer, including the orbit work of its day.

Decell opens by fixing notation for inverses, transposes, and range spaces, then states his aim plainly. The paper investigates how to invert matrices that are singular or not even square. It gives a new algorithm for computing the generalized inverse of any complex matrix. For a matrix that does have an ordinary inverse, the algorithm simply returns that inverse.
nasa-tm-19710013146-subsonic-aerodynamic:
William P Henderson of the Langley Research Center studied a highly swept fixed wing shape at low speed. Tests ran in the Langley high speed seven by ten foot tunnel. The team varied the wing dihedral angle, the upward tilt of the wings. They also changed vertical tails, tail cant, and leading edge flap settings.

Runs covered a Mach number of 0.168 and a wide range of attack angles. Adding the vertical tails improved the static stability of the shape. Instability then held off until a higher lift level. Data of this kind helped designers judge swept wing layouts. Such wings were central to planned fast aircraft of the period.
nasa-tm-19710016707-low-speed-aerodynami:
Anthony M. Cook and Thomas N. Aiken of the Ames Research Center issued this memorandum in March 1971, as NASA TM X-62,017. It reports low-speed wind tunnel tests of a large model of a STOL transport, an aircraft built for short takeoffs and landings. The model carried an augmented jet flap, which boosts lift by blowing engine air through the wing flap.

The tests used configurations picked earlier for landing approach and takeoff, aimed at a proposed flight research aircraft based on the CV-7A Buffalo. The team varied the thrust of the underwing engines and its direction, and measured fuselage boundary-layer control effects. Several lateral control methods were also tried to measure roll control power. Runs were made with and without the horizontal tail in the Ames forty-by-eighty-foot wind tunnel.
nasa-tm-19720016361-large-scale-wind-tun:
Michael D Falarski of the Ames Research Center and the Army Air Mobility laboratory reported this large tunnel study in May 1972, as NASA TM X-62,154. The report runs to one hundred eighteen pages. Its model was half of a wing, over fourteen feet across. A ducted fan blew air over its flap for lift. Such externally blown flaps promised short takeoffs, but they were loud. Falarski measured the noise in detail.

The fan measured thirty inches across and ran at gentle pressure. Flap size changed between test series. The fan's height above the wing also varied. Each change's effect on the sound was recorded. Big models give noise data close to real aircraft scale. The results served the quiet short haul transport effort.
nasa-tm-19720025115-aerodynamic-and-acou:
Brent A. Miller and John M. Abbott wrote this NASA memorandum at the Lewis Research Center in September 1972. They tested two engine inlets, the openings that guide air into a jet fan. Both inlets could choke, or narrow, the flow of air passing through them.

One inlet choked flow by sliding its center body along its axis. The other used a moving grid of small airfoils. The pair ran choked and open, across a range of air flows. Miller and Abbott measured pressure, flow quality, and fan noise. Choking cut fan blade noise by a large margin. Such work pointed toward quieter jet engines.
new-ideas-in-india-during-the-nineteenth:
John Morrison, late principal of the General Assembly's Institution in Calcutta, published New Ideas in India in London in 1907. Macmillan issued the book in London and New York. Morrison had also sat in the senate of Calcutta University. The work began under a lectureship at Edinburgh on science, philosophy, and kindred study.

Chapters open with the new era and Indian conservatism, then new social ideas. One asks what chief thing dissolved the old ideas, and another treats woman's place. Political chapters cover a uniting India and false patriotism. Religious chapters ask if new ideas exist there, then survey Indian Christians, Brahmas, Aryas, and Theosophists.
on-the-spanish-main-or-some-english-fora:
John Masefield published this sea history in London in 1906. Methuen issued the book with twenty-two pictures and a map. Masefield dedicates it to artist Jack B. Yeats. Chapter one tells Drake's voyage to the West Indies. Drake's quarrel with the Spaniards opens the story.

The subtitle promises English forays on the Isthmus of Darien. Masefield also describes the buccaneers who raided there. Old-time ships and sailors receive a short account. Captain William Dampier fronts the book in a portrait. Masefield writes history with a poet's love of the sea. The book suits readers of pirate and exploration tales.
pennsylvania-pilgrim-and-other-poems-par:
John Greenleaf Whittier's narrative poem The Pennsylvania Pilgrim tells of the German Pietists who settled near Philadelphia. An introductory note explains that German emigration to America began with William Penn's 1677 visit to the Continent. There he met the circle of mystics gathered around the pastor Spener.

That circle formed the Frankfort Land Company, which bought Pennsylvania land from Penn. Its agent was Francis Daniel Pastorius, the young lawyer who led the settlers. This part of Whittier's works pairs the long title poem with shorter narrative pieces such as King Volmer and Elsie and The Witch of Wenham.
personal-narrative-of-travels-to-the-equ: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of volume 2 of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, the Bohn's Scientific Library title pages, with no travel text visible. The title page names Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland. It gives their travels to the equinoctial regions of America during 1799 to 1804, translated from the French and edited by Thomasina Ross. This London edition of George Bell and Sons is dated 1907, and notes on local measures, the tablon and the torta, follow the title pages.
richard-van-der-borght-the-facts-in-the-: The Facts in the Case of the Horrible Murder of Little Myrtle Vance, by Richard van der Borght. The murder's facts. This book preserves that pamphlet. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it.
the-adventures-of-col-daniel-boon-contai: John Filson's 1784 narrative, the book that made Daniel Boone a legend. Part biography, part adventure, it tells of the Wilderness Road, the founding of Boonesborough, and wars with the Shawnee, in Boone's own reported voice. The founding text of the American frontier myth, and a genuine historical source.
the-church-and-the-empire-being-an-outli: Dudley Medley outlines the church's history from 1003 — its tangled relations with empire and state. His clear survey serves students well. A useful short history of a vast subject. Popes, emperors, and reformers cross his well-ordered stage. Students have long prized his lucid, fair-minded summary.
the-conditions-of-existence-as-affecting: What keeps living things alive? Huxley names their needs: food, luck, and few foes. Nature drives a hard bargain with all her children. The price of survival, put in plain words, the price of survival, put in plain words.
the-history-of-henry-esmond-esq-a-colone: Thackeray's 1852 novel follows Henry Esmond from a troubled youth to Queen Anne's court. Written as a memoir, it is the most graceful historical novel in English. Noble, sad, and wise: his greatest book. Thackeray wrote it in the Queen Anne style he loved.
the-little-book-of-modern-verse-a-select: Jessie Rittenhouse's 1913 anthology of modern verse: the new poetry of the 1910s, selected with taste. A snapshot of American poetry on the eve of modernism. Charming and historically interesting. Rittenhouse's taste caught the new poetry at its freshest.
the-pocket-r-l-s-being-favourite-passage: A pocketful of Stevenson: the best passages from his tales and essays, chosen for travelers. Treasure Island's spirit in miniature. The essential R.L.S., sized for the coat pocket. Stevenson for the pocket and the heart.
the-second-book-of-modern-verse-a-select: Jessie Rittenhouse's second anthology of modern verse: more of the new poetry, selected with a sure hand. The 1910s' poetic ferment continues. A worthy companion to her first book. The modernist wave was gathering as this book appeared.
